data: © NASA/JPL-Caltech — Gale Crater landing site; nuclear-powered rover (RTG), still operational.

Mars Science Laboratory. RTG-powered (no solar reliance), car-sized (899 kg), still operational over a decade after landing. Confirmed Gale Crater hosted a habitable lake environment in the deep past. Climbing Mt. Sharp's stratigraphic sequence — billion-year-by-billion-year readings of Mars's environmental history.
First nuclear-powered Mars rover; first to confirm a past habitable environment on Mars.

NASA's Curiosity rover launched November 26, 2011 atop an Atlas V from Cape Canaveral. After 254 days of cruise, Mars Science Laboratory delivered the 899-kg nuclear-powered rover to Gale Crater on August 6, 2012 via the now-famous sky-crane landing. More than a decade later Curiosity is still climbing Mount Sharp, drilling rocks that hold a record of Mars's once-habitable past.
Building a rover for Gale Crater
Mars Science Laboratory assembled at JPL — Curiosity, descent stage, backshell + heat shield stacked for shipment to Florida.
The MMRTG nuclear power source (orange disk, lower right) provides ~110 W continuously for ≥14 years — no solar panels, no winter shutdowns.
November 26, 2011 — Atlas V from Cape Canaveral
Atlas V 541 lifts off from SLC-41 carrying Mars Science Laboratory + Curiosity. 10:02 EST, November 26 2011.
Mont Mercou panorama, sol 3070 (March 2021). Mastcam-Z 360° sweep showing the rover, the layered cliffs of Mt Mercou, and Mount Sharp on the horizon.
HiRISE overhead view of Curiosity's traverse, captured by Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter at 25 cm/pixel.
Self-portrait at "Big Sky" drill site, sol 1126 — composite of dozens of MAHLI close-ups stitched into a single image.
Evidence of an ancient habitable Mars
Drill hole at Yellowknife Bay — the first sample from Mars's past lake-bed environment, January 2013.
Sedimentary rocks at Vera Rubin Ridge — banded iron formations + clay minerals indicate ancient liquid water and a habitable chemical environment.
JPL mission control celebrates the seven-minutes-of-terror sky-crane landing, August 5/6 2012 — Adam Steltzner and team after the first signals from Gale Crater.

Illustrated block map of Curiosity’s route across Gale Crater: from Bradbury Landing (sol 0) past the John Klein drill site (sol 182), Marias Pass (sol 992), Murray Buttes (sol 1451), Vera Rubin Ridge (sol 1805) and Greenheugh Pediment (sol 3413) to the rover’s position at sol 5045, with the way on to Mount Sharp.
